label: 2026 年第 34 期
title: 证明你是人
intro: 这一期围着身份转：谁算人、谁被记下、谁被相信。默认先看一类；要看整期，点最后的「全部」。

articles.title: Samuel Beckett’s German Diaries
articles.summary: 贝克特 1936–37 年德国日记首次出版：他不是不问政治的人，只是把恐惧写在本子里。
articles.briefing:
The publication of Samuel Beckett's German diaries is not a literary sidecar. It is a record of a young writer walking through a country that was already rehearsing its future, and of a man who later joined the French Resistance taking notes while paper was still a private risk. Six notebooks from September 1936 to April 1937, covering a tour of some thirty German cities, appear for the first time on 20 August 2026 from Suhrkamp, in a bilingual edition edited by Mark Nixon and Oliver Lubrich. The book runs to 545 pages and about 120,000 words. The notebooks themselves sat in a Paris cellar until after Beckett's death in 1989. An English edition is expected next April. That delay belongs to the story. These were private pages, written where a diary could be confiscated, and they have taken nearly ninety years to become a public argument about whether the author of the late plays was as politically vacant as a certain piety likes to claim.

The argument they make is against a convenient Beckett. The later work can look as if politics has been boiled off: a road, a tree, two men waiting, language thinning toward silence. The diaries do not allow that reading to stand as a biography. Beckett watched Hitler's crowds and wrote a sentence that is neither a slogan nor a joke: "They'll need to fight soon (or burst)." He collected Nazi phrases the way a linguist collects a dialect, which is also the way a careful man collects evidence that the air has changed. He noticed the "Hitler coat." He stuck the wrong arm out instead of giving the salute. These are not acts of heroism. They are the small, bodily refusals of someone who is depressed, in psychoanalysis, and cautious because notebooks can be seized. The caution is itself political. A writer who knows his pages might be read by the wrong official is already living inside a police aesthetic. The later Resistance work does not retroactively turn every 1936 sentence into a manifesto. It does mean that the man who wrote Waiting for Godot had already practiced a form of attention that refused to look away.

The personal weather is not decoration. His cousin Peggy Sinclair had died of tuberculosis in 1933. Her family, of Jewish descent, fled in 1936, the year the German tour began. Beckett is not drifting through museums in a vacuum. He is moving through a country that is already sorting people into those who may stay and those who must leave, and he is related to people in the second column. The diaries do not make him a prophet. They make him a witness who was also a patient, a cousin, a young man with a coat and a wrong arm. Nixon and Lubrich have to do the historian's unglamorous work: date, annotate, refuse the myth that genius floats above the street. The bilingual page is a reminder that Beckett's languages were already a politics. He wrote in a Germany that was inventing a new public speech, and he stole samples of it.

If this issue is about who counts as a person, and who gets believed, the diaries are an early file. A man writes because he is not sure he will be allowed to say it later. The notebooks survived a cellar. The people he was related to had to survive a border. What the Suhrkamp edition asks of a reader in 2026 is not piety toward a Nobel saint. It is a slower account of how a mind records a regime before the regime has finished becoming itself. Read the Guardian piece, then sit with the edition when the English pages arrive. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: Beckett was not above politics. He was taking notes in a country that would soon make notes lethal.

articles.title: How art invented humanity
articles.summary: 不是人发明了艺术，是艺术把人变成了人：马特尔从拉斯科写到美与真，拒绝把洞穴壁画讲成寓言。
articles.briefing:
J. F. Martel's Aeon essay begins in a place that has been photographed until it looks like a brand, and then asks you to unlearn the postcard. Lascaux, near Montignac, was found in 1940 by teenagers. The paintings are about twenty thousand years old, which is already a humility: older art exists elsewhere, and the French cave is not the origin of the species. What Lascaux still does, if you let it, is rearrange the usual sentence about culture. We like to say that humans invented art once they had spare time, spare calories, and a self to express. Martel's thesis runs the other way. Art invented humanity. The capacity to make and to be claimed by images is not a decoration on an already finished animal. It is one of the ways the animal became the kind of creature that can have a history.

The essay refuses the just-so story that cave art exists to explain hunting, or fertility, or a lesson for the young. Those stories are not always false. They are too small. They treat the paintings as a PowerPoint from the Pleistocene. Martel would rather keep the strangeness intact. There is an apocryphal Picasso line — "We have invented nothing" — which may never have been said in a studio and still names a feeling people have in front of those walls: later technique looks like a footnote. Keats, standing before a Grecian urn, made beauty and truth change places. Werner Herzog, filming in another cave, split "the truth of accountants" from "ecstatic truth." Van Gogh's Wheatfield with Crows is not a weather report. It is a mind using paint to make a world that was not already there. None of these citations is a proof. They are a tradition of people admitting that the image does something prior to the argument we later hang on it.

Martel is not anti-science. He is suspicious of a science that forgets its own wonder. The intelligibility of the universe — the fact that mathematics and experiment keep working — is itself a mystery, not a solvent that dissolves every other mystery. He distinguishes two beauties that modern taste keeps trying to collapse. There is the geometer's beauty: symmetry, proportion, the elegance of a law. And there is the singular, the bizarre, the beauty Baudelaire knew how to praise, which does not generalise and does not want to. Cave art is closer to the second. A particular horse, a particular twist of horn, a particular use of a bulge in the rock: these are not illustrations of "the horse." They are encounters. If you reduce them to a function, you have already left the cave.

The claim that art invented us is easy to parody. It can sound like a museum wall text with incense. Martel's useful stubbornness is methodological. Do not start with a theory of early religion and then go looking for pictures that fit. Start with the fact that people went into the earth and made something that still stops a later species in its tracks. The making is not a hobby that appeared after we became human. It is part of how personhood got practiced: a being that can be addressed by an image is already different from a being that only eats and flees. This issue keeps asking who counts as a person. Martel's answer is not legal. It is aesthetic in the old sense. A person is among other things a creature that can be altered by a wall.

Read the original when you have a long sitting. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room. Aeon will take you through the full walk, including the parts a digest would only flatten.

articles.title: Why make art in the dark?
articles.summary: 祖先为什么摸黑进洞作画？维舍不信一个总理论，只信火光、回声、触觉，以及视觉在黑暗里会骗人。
articles.briefing:
Izzy Wisher's question is almost rude in its simplicity. Why go deep underground, with fire lamps, to make images that almost no one would see in daylight? Las Chimeneas, in northern Spain, holds stags about eighteen thousand years old. The conservator Eduardo Palacio-Pérez works in a space that is not a gallery and not a temple in any sense we can certify. Upper Palaeolithic people chose the dark on purpose. They carried light that flickered. They heard their own breath come back as echo. They touched rock that had a temperature and a dampness a photograph cannot store. Wisher's essay is a case against the single key that unlocks all of this. The dark is not a riddle with one answer. It is an environment.

The usual hypotheses arrive on cue, and she lets them in without letting them rule. Shamanism has had a long run in cave-art studies: the images as traces of trance, the cave as a membrane to another world. The theory has been criticised for doing too much work with too little constraint, for turning every painted animal into a spirit and every bend in the passage into a cosmology. Proto-writing and seasonal signs offer a different tidiness: marks as information, a calendar in pigment, the beginning of a record. Art for art's sake offers a third tidiness, which is the refusal of function. Each of these can be true in a given case. None of them deserves a monopoly. Wisher prefers accounts that stay multisensory. Flicker changes what a line is. Echo changes what a ceremony is, if ceremony is even the right word. Touch changes what a wall is. A theory that only asks what the pictures "mean" has already discarded half the event.

Vision, in peripheral darkness, is a poor witness. The eye invents. Pareidolia — the habit of finding faces and beasts in stains and shadows — is not a modern glitch. It is what human sight does when the world is underlit. A lamp that moves will make a crack become a flank and then become a crack again. If you are looking for a master motive, this unreliability is an embarrassment. If you are looking for an experience, it is the point. People may have gone into the caves partly because the dark would collaborate: the rock would offer animals, the flame would animate them, the mind would complete them. That is not the same as saying the art is an accident. It is saying that the makers were working with a medium that included their own nervous system.

Sit with the experience rather than one master theory: that is Wisher's discipline, and it is harder than it sounds. A magazine culture likes a thesis you can carry out of the cave. Ancestral psychology likes a just-so story. Wisher asks for something closer to fieldwork of the senses. You do not have to reject explanation. You have to stop pretending that explanation is the same as having been there. Palacio-Pérez, working as a conservator among the Chimeneas stags, is a reminder that the images now have a second life as objects that must be kept from our breath and our lamps. The original makers accepted flicker. We send in specialists to stop time. Read after Martel if you want the pair. He argues that art invented humanity. She asks what kind of art, in what kind of dark, with what kind of body. The two essays do not cancel. They keep the pictures from becoming either a slogan about the human or a footnote in a textbook on hunting magic. A person, in this week's sense, is also a perceiving animal that can be fooled by its own eye and still choose the dark on purpose.

Read the original on Aeon. This briefing is the stance, not the walk: the dark was not a storage room. It was part of the work.

articles.title: Inside Russia’s New Gulag
articles.summary: 纽约客走进罗斯托夫看守所：战争把俄国监狱系统改造成了关押乌克兰人的新古拉格。
articles.briefing:
The New Yorker's report from inside Russia's rebuilt prison system is not a history lecture on Stalin, and it should not be read as one. The word gulag arrives with a century of images. This piece needs a colder attention. After the February 2022 invasion, Ukrainian soldiers and civilians have been held for alleged crimes against Russia. The architecture is old; the purpose is current. SIZO-1 in Rostov is an E-shaped jail from the era of Catherine the Great. A building can outlast the regime that stacked its bricks and still be put to a new kind of work. The story is reportage on a prison system remade for a war: who is taken, where they are sent, what the cells do to a body, and what a child is told when a mother disappears into the map.

The squalor is not a metaphor. In a Donetsk jail, conditions were filthy enough that women said they were rotting alive. Iryna Mohitych, who had cooked for Azov, is one of the people who put that sentence into the record. "We were rotting alive" is not a literary flourish. It is a description of damp, neglect, and time used as an instrument. The piece follows lives that do not fit a single prisoner category. Some of the detained were combatants. Some were civilians swept into a legal machinery that treats the fact of being Ukrainian, or of having been in the wrong place, as the beginning of a case. The alleged crimes are against Russia. The geography of punishment is Russian: investigation prisons, colonies, the long eastward haul that has always been part of how this state makes people vanish without needing to shoot them on the first day.

Yulia Vlasova was four when her mother, Natalia, was arrested. Natalia is now in a Siberian colony. A child that age does not have a theory of international law. She has an absence that will last longer than the news cycle that produced it. The detail belongs in a digest because it keeps the article from becoming a tour of architecture. Catherine's E-shaped jail is a good opening image. The girl is the cost. A war that holds civilians and soldiers in the same expanding system is not only fighting at the front. It is manufacturing a population of the disappeared, the sentenced, the transferred, and the children who will grow up around a missing name. Reportage of this kind is slow on purpose. It has to establish what can be known, what survivors will say, and what the state will not.

Readers who want the Stalin comparison will find it waiting. Resist the cheap version. The historical gulag was a civilisation of camps with its own economics and its own literature. What the New Yorker is describing is a contemporary apparatus: wartime charges, filtration, the reuse of old shells of stone, the movement of Ukrainian prisoners into the Russian interior. Continuity of cruelty is not the same as identity of system. The useful inheritance from the older literature is a method — name the place, name the person, refuse the state's story about why the cage is necessary — not a license to collapse 2026 into 1937. This issue is about who is recorded as a person and who is filed as a problem. A prison system is a filing system with locks.

Read the original when you have a long sitting. The magazine's job is the full walk: the cells, the transfers, the voices that got out. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room. It is a war story told from the inside of a jail.

articles.title: To save the asylum system, reform it
articles.summary: 庇护作为战后法律承诺正在崩：要救这个制度，就得改革，而不是把避难本身废掉。
articles.briefing:
The postwar asylum system was a legal promise dressed as a moral one: people fleeing persecution would have a place to make a claim, and states would hear it. The Economist's by-invitation essay starts from the fact that the promise is collapsing under conditions it was not built to handle. Mixed flows — refugees and economic migrants arriving through the same routes — have blurred the category the law needs in order to work. Smuggling has industrialised the crossing. Courts are slow. Politics has turned the delay into a weapon. None of this is an argument for abolishing refuge. It is an argument that a right without a working process becomes a slogan, and a slogan cannot protect anyone.

The typical Economist line is easy to caricature and still worth stating cleanly. Distinguish people who need protection from people who are moving for work. Decide cases fast enough that the decision is real. Cooperate on returns when a claim fails, or the failed claim becomes a settlement by other means. Keep a legal path, because if the legal path is a rumour, the illegal one wins. The essay is not a humanitarian pamphlet and not a nativist tract. It is a piece about institutions that lose legitimacy when they cannot do the job on the door. Compassion without a process tells the public that feeling is a policy. Cruelty without a process is simply cruelty. The live political danger is that publics, watching both the chaos and the sermons, will choose the second and call it realism.

Reform, in this register, is a conservative act. You change the machinery so that the underlying commitment can survive contact with numbers, boats, and elections. That will offend readers who think any distinction between refugee and migrant is a betrayal, and it will offend readers who think the commitment itself is the mistake. The essay's wager is that those two camps, left to themselves, will finish the job of destroying asylum from opposite sides. One side makes every arrival a sacred exception and then wonders why voters revolt. The other side makes every arrival a threat and then wonders why the next disaster produces people with nowhere legal to go. A system that cannot tell the difference between a person fleeing a secret police and a person chasing wages will eventually treat both as a border problem.

This issue keeps returning to proof: who is believed, who is recorded, who is allowed to stay in the category "person with a claim." Asylum is one of the last official rituals in which a state is supposed to listen to a stranger's story and then bind itself. When the ritual takes years, the story rots, the smuggler profits, and the politician discovers that contempt is popular. When the ritual is abolished, the stranger has no story that counts. Mixed flows make the listening harder, which is not a reason to stop listening; it is a reason to get faster at telling protection from a labour journey, and honest about the difference. The Economist is not going to give you a novelist's account of a particular crossing, and it will not hand you a table of invented percentages. It is going to give you the institutional argument. Read it as that. Then decide whether you think the promise can be saved by being made narrower and faster, or whether "reform" is the polite word for retreat. A working process is the only form compassion can take once a queue exists.

Read the original. This briefing is here so the tension is already in the room: a refuge that cannot decide is not kinder than a refuge that decides.

articles.title: Resist the technocrats
articles.summary: 要保住真正的专业判断，先抵抗把政治决定伪装成中立专家意见的技术官僚国际。
articles.briefing:
Jan Eijking's Aeon essay, drawn from his 2026 book The Technocratic International, is a rescue mission with an unfashionable target. He wants to save expertise. To do that, he says, you have to resist technocracy. The two are constantly sold as the same thing: people who know, therefore people who should decide. International organisations have lived on that sale. They present themselves as the place where impartial experts rule, above the mess of parliaments and crowds. Eijking's cut is simple and unkind to that self-image. Expertise is a form of knowledge that can be argued with. Technocracy is a political style that uses experts to depoliticise decisions and dodge accountability. The civil servants of the international world are often very good at the second while claiming the prestige of the first.

The historical demythologising matters. International organisations were never beyond politics. They were built inside an unequal order and they protected it. The language of neutrality — standards, best practice, the committee that merely implements — is a way of making a settlement look like weather. Once a decision has been described as technical, the people it binds are invited to have feelings but not arguments. That is convenient for governments that would rather not defend a bargain in public, and convenient for officials who would rather not be voted out. Eijking is not asking you to join a revolt against science. He is asking you to notice when "the science" or "the experts" are being used as a screen. The target is not the epidemiologist, the engineer, or the trade lawyer. The target is the move that says: because someone competent has spoken, the rest of us may now stop talking.

This is a distinction a university reader should already want. You can believe that some questions have better and worse answers, and still believe that the choice of which question to ask is political. You can want competent people in the room and still want to know who appointed them, whom they answer to, and what happens when they are wrong. Technocracy's trick is to collapse those levels. A model becomes a mandate. A secretariat becomes a sovereign. When the public finally notices, the backlash is stupid in the usual way: it attacks "experts" as a class, including the ones who were trying to describe a fact. Eijking's warning is that if you do not separate the categories, you will lose the first while fighting the second.

The essay belongs in a week about proof and personhood because technocracy is a theory of who may speak. The expert is heard as a person. The public is heard as noise, or as data. Resist that, and you are not embracing ignorance. You are insisting that a decision which allocates risk, money, and status has to come back into a place where it can be opposed. International organisations will still be needed. Borders, viruses, and capital do not respect the map. What they should not be allowed is the claim that their origins were innocent and their procedures are merely rational. Eijking's book title is a diagnosis: the technocratic international is a style of rule, not a library of facts. Demythologise the origins, and the present gets easier to argue with. Read him for the book-length version of a sentence this digest can only post on the door: to save expertise, stop letting technocrats hide inside it. The civil servant who "merely implements" is still a political animal. The courtesy is to say so before the backlash says it stupidly.

Read the original on Aeon. This briefing is the cut. The essay is the history that makes the cut cost something.

articles.title: The Delusions of John Roberts
articles.summary: 罗伯茨得到了他想要的法院；塔尔博特问：当总统开始感谢这份权力，制度主义者还剩什么。
articles.briefing:
Margaret Talbot's New Yorker profile of John Roberts is a study in a man who got what he wanted and may not survive the gift. Roberts has long been cast, and has cast himself, as an institutionalist: a Chief Justice who cares about the Court's legitimacy, its appearance of being above the daily fight, the long life of the building rather than the short life of a coalition. Look at the docket of the last several years and the institutionalist has been busy. The administrative state is weaker. The presidency is stronger. Affirmative action and voting-rights protections have been rolled back. These were not accidents that happened to him. They are a constitutional mood he helped install. The profile's cruel question is what happens when the president who benefits from that mood is a man likely to abuse the extra room.

Donald Trump wanted to attend oral argument in Trump v. Barbara, a case about birthright citizenship and the Fourteenth Amendment, with Wong Kim Ark of 1898 in the background. No president had sat in on the Court's arguments. The request is almost a genre painting of the present: a head of state treating the courtroom as a box at the theatre, the legal question being who counts as a citizen at birth, the historical ghost being a man born in San Francisco to Chinese parents whose claim the Court once accepted. Whether Trump is in the room or not, the case is about personhood in the most official American sense. Who is born into the polity. Who can be written out by a new reading. Roberts, if he is the institutionalist of the brochures, should flinch at a president using the argument as a stage. The profile suggests a worse possibility: that flinching is no longer the main risk.

For an institutionalist, Trump's gratitude when the Court helps him may be worse than his attacks. Attacks can be answered with marble language about independence. Gratitude implies a relationship. It turns a judgment into a favour. It teaches the public, and the president, that the Court is a faction that sometimes comes through. Roberts has spent a career trying to keep the institution looking like a court. The doctrines he has midwifed — more room for the executive, less room for agencies, a narrower reading of racial remedies — now sit in front of an executive who does not share Roberts's taste for the appearance of restraint. You can believe those doctrines are correct as law and still see the political fact. Power does not stay where a theorist left it. It goes where the next occupant can take it.

Talbot is writing a person, not a treatise. The delusions of the title are not only ideological. They are the occupational hazard of a man who thinks that if the opinions are crafted finely enough, the building will remain a building. Birthright citizenship is a useful stress test because it is not a technicality. It is a rule about who is already one of us before anyone has filled in a form. Wong Kim Ark was the older Court's answer to a panic about Chinese birth. The new case asks whether that answer still binds. A Chief Justice who expanded presidential power and then faces a president eager to sit in the gallery is living inside his own success. Read the profile for the texture: the man, the court, the case, the gratitude that may be more corrosive than the rage.

Read the original when you have a long sitting. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room. An institutionalist who wins can still lose the institution.

articles.title: The Fearless Charge of Morocco’s Horsewomen
articles.summary: 摩洛哥女骑手闯进男人的马上火枪表演：人少、自费，已经改写了谁能并排冲锋。
articles.briefing:
Tbourida, also called fantasia, is a cavalry display with a sixteenth-century pedigree and a UNESCO listing: riders gallop in a line and fire together, the point being not a duel but a single crash of sound and dust. For most of its life the line was male. National Geographic's feature, with reporting that draws on the explorer Gwyneth Talley and on photographs by Chantal Pinzi in her Farīsāt series, is about the women who have been forcing their way into that line since the mid-2000s. The timing is not mystical. Morocco's 2004 family-code reforms changed the legal weather around what women could claim in public. The sociologist Zakia Salime has called what followed a "quiet revolution." Tbourida is one of the noisier rooms in which that quiet has become visible.

The names matter because a "women's troupe" can sound like a programme. Zahia Aboulait was a pioneer and is now a mentor. Bouchra Nabata founded a troupe in 2007. They are not a mass movement if you count heads. Against something like a thousand troupes in the country, there may be a dozen women's groups; other counts put the women's share even smaller, seven among a few hundred. Either way the arithmetic is the same. This is a small minority riding inside a heritage that was built to look eternal and male. The riders often pay for their own horses, costumes, and the permits that make gunpowder legal. Heritage, when it is not a state pageant, is an expensive hobby. The women are not being issued a revolution. They are buying the right to be in the picture.

What the charge does, if you watch it as politics rather than folklore, is rewrite who is allowed to be spectacular. Tbourida is a performance of coordination and nerve. The line has to hold. The shots have to land together. A woman in that geometry is not asking for a separate, softer art. She is doing the same dangerous thing and making the audience adjust its idea of the past. Pinzi's photographs matter here. A still of a rider in costume can be consumed as exoticism. A series that stays with the work — the animals, the powder, the waiting — makes it harder to file the women as a tourist extra. Talley's presence as a National Geographic Explorer is a reminder that this is also a research beat: how a living heritage absorbs a new kind of body without admitting that the heritage was ever a rule about bodies.

This issue is about who gets to count as a person in a public ritual. A cavalry display is a ritual of belonging. For centuries the belonging was gendered in the saddle. The family-code climate did not automatically put women on horses. People did that, at their own expense, in a country that still has a thousand reasons to call the old line the real one. Aboulait teaching the next riders, Nabata keeping a troupe alive since 2007: these are institutions built at the scale of a stable, not a ministry. The gunpowder permit is a bureaucratic joke that is also a fact of the work. Read the original for the faces, the dust, and Pinzi's photographs, which a briefing should not try to restage. The argument is already simple. The charge was never only about horses. It was about who may ride at the front of a nation's idea of itself, and who has to pay for the costume to be believed.

Read the National Geographic piece. This briefing is here so you know what kind of story it is: not a mascot, a minority rewriting a heritage from inside the line.

articles.title: Hannah Arendt’s American Education
articles.summary: 阿伦特 1941 年身无分文抵达纽约；丹比写她如何在一个会改写历史的世界里学会判断。
articles.briefing:
David Denby's New Yorker essay, working from Thomas Meyer's book and from the long American afterlife of Hannah Arendt, begins with an arrival that is almost too emblematic to use and too true to skip. In May 1941 Arendt reached New York on a Portuguese refugee ship, stateless, broke, and weak in English, with Heinrich Blücher. She had been interned in France. She was carrying the manuscript of Walter Benjamin's Theses. The inventory is not a costume drama. It is the material condition of a thinker who would spend the rest of her life writing about what happens to people when the legal world withdraws its recognition and when governments start to rewrite the past as a method of rule. America was not a theory she packed. It was a country she had to learn, in a language she did not yet own, after Europe had tried to make her a non-person.

Denby is not writing a cradle-to-grave. The useful centre, for a reader of this issue, is Arendt on lying governments. When history is constantly rewritten, she argued, people lose the capacity to act, to think, and to judge. The sentence is easy to quote at a dinner. It is harder to keep in its severity. A lie about yesterday is not only an insult to the record. It is an attack on the faculties that make a public possible. If you cannot trust that what happened remains available, you cannot deliberate. If you cannot deliberate, you cannot act as a citizen rather than as a spectator of whoever is currently holding the microphone. Arendt's American education included discovering a republic that still talked as if those faculties were ordinary, while she arrived with the European knowledge of how quickly they can be abolished.

Personhood, in her work, is never only a passport. It is the standing that lets a human being appear among others and be answered. Statelessness had taught her what it means when that standing is gone: you may still have a body, a language, a lover, a manuscript in a bag, and still have no place from which a claim can be heard. The Benjamin pages in that bag are not a sentimental relic. They are a thinker's last theses travelling in another thinker's luggage, which is already a theory of how thought survives when institutions do not. Denby, reading Meyer and the American Arendt, is interested in how she became a public figure in a country that had not made her, and how the country became a laboratory for her questions about freedom, evil, and the life of the mind.

Do not ask this briefing for extra biography. The facts that matter here are the ones the piece gives: the ship, the poverty, the internment, the English that had to be acquired, the companion, the manuscript, the argument about political lying. Connect them lightly to the week's theme and they click without being forced. Proof of being human is not only a scan of an iris. It is also whether a polity will still let you judge, and whether the past is stable enough that judgment has an object. Meyer's book and the American years are Denby's occasion; the occasion is enough. A stateless arrival is an education whether or not the student asked for it. Read him for the books and the tone. This briefing is only the door: a woman arrives without a state and spends decades explaining what that absence does to everyone else, including the people who thought they were safely documented.

Read the original when you have a sitting. The New Yorker's job is the full encounter with Meyer and with Arendt in America. The argument is already in the room.

articles.title: The US-Saudi nuclear deal raises radioactive questions
articles.summary: 美沙民用核协议从来不只关电：谁浓缩、谁核查、这笔买卖在政治上买到了什么。
articles.briefing:
A civil nuclear bargain with Saudi Arabia is never only about electricity. That is the first sentence the Economist's by-invitation essay needs you to accept before the rest of the questions will sit still. Reactors make power. They also make a fuel cycle, a set of inspection problems, a regional signal toward Iran, and a vendor contest in which American firms are not the only people in the room. China is in that room, which means the deal is also a choice about whose engineers, whose fuel services, and whose political intimacy will last the thirty-year life of a plant. "Atoms for peace" is the old American phrase for spreading civilian nuclear technology while trying to keep the military use locked away. Whether the phrase still describes a workable order, or only a nostalgia, is the weather around any new deal. A reader who wants only a story about megawatts has already left the article.

The live questions are not a treaty text this briefing will invent. Who enriches? Enrichment is the hinge between a power programme and a pathway that makes other capitals nervous. A kingdom that can buy reactors but not the ability to concentrate fuel is a customer. A kingdom that can enrich is a different kind of counterpart, whatever the stated purpose. Who inspects? Inspections are the difference between a peaceful programme and a programme that asks the world to take its word. The International Atomic Energy Agency is the usual name in this sentence; the politics is about how much access a sovereign will grant, and how much a supplier will demand as the price of components and diplomatic cover. What does the bargain buy politically? Electricity is the public good. The private goods may include security guarantees, a position against Iran, a win for a particular vendor, a demonstration that Washington can still close a deal in a region where it has been losing the habit.

Vendor competition is not a footnote. Nuclear plants are decades-long relationships: fuel, parts, training, debt, and a political intimacy that outlasts the minister who cut the ribbon. If American firms lose the contract, they do not only lose revenue. The United States loses a channel. If they win it on terms that go soft on enrichment or inspections, they may win a channel that later looks like a proliferation story. Iran sits at the edge of every paragraph, not because Riyadh and Tehran are the same case, but because regional nuclear status is relational. One programme is read as an answer to another. The essay's job is to keep those readings in view without pretending that a civil deal is innocent because the press release says "power."

This is filed under 经济 because it is a bargain: technology, capital, and statecraft in a single invoice. It also belongs in a week about who is trusted. A nuclear agreement is a ceremony of trust with Geiger counters. Atoms for peace was always a bargain of this kind — electricity in one hand, a non-proliferation story in the other — and the essay's doubt is whether the old bargain still binds when the vendors have multiplied and the region already contains a nuclear argument with Iran. Read the original for the invitation's full case. Do not expect this digest to supply clauses that were not given, or a fake annex of limits and sunset dates. Expect it to keep the questions radioactive, which is to say alive: who enriches, who inspects, and what the politics thinks it has purchased when the lights come on. A civil programme that cannot answer those three is not civilian enough to be boring.

Read the Economist piece. This briefing is the list of questions. The essay is where they get their weight.

articles.title: The Taliban are vile. Democracies must still engage with them
articles.summary: 孤立塔利班五年几乎无效；经济学人说：不必承认他们正确，但必须继续打交道。
articles.briefing:
The Economist's leader is a sentence that many readers will hate and still have to finish. The Taliban are vile. Democracies must still engage with them. Isolation — no recognition, frozen reserves, sanctions — has achieved almost nothing in five years, which is long enough that "give it time" has become a way of not looking at the result. Hardliners do not need Western investors. They need the country they already hold, and they have it. The movement is not going away. Russia has recognised them. China, India, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates deal on mining and trade. The West's moral boycott has not produced a more decent Kabul. It has produced a capital that does business with other people, on terms those people will write.

Recognition is not approval. That distinction is the leader's load-bearing wall, and it is the one domestic politics likes to flatten. To recognise a government is to admit a fact about control, to open a channel, to put diplomats in a position to watch terrorism and to talk when talking is ugly. It is not a certificate of virtue. Embassies, where they still function as listening posts, are instruments of statecraft rather than of endorsement. The alternative is to let the watching be done only by states that have fewer scruples and more appetite for lithium, copper, and a corridor. Reform, if it comes, will come from inside, and it may take decades. Outsiders who imagine that a tighter freeze will midwife a different regime are arguing with a fantasy of leverage. The leverage was spent, or was never as large as the speeches.

This is filed under 经济 because isolation is an economic policy pretending to be a moral holiday. Frozen reserves, sanctions, and the absence of Western capital are choices about who may extract, who may bank, and who sets the price of contact. When democracies leave the room, the room does not stay empty. It fills with buyers who do not ask about girls' schools as a condition of a mining memorandum. Embassies, in the leader's account, are there to watch terrorism and to keep a channel, not to bless the regime's idea of a woman. The leader's coldness is the point. Hold your nose and talk. The nose-holding is not optional; the talking is not a reward. A state that cannot distinguish engagement from applause will keep choosing isolation and then act surprised when isolation fails.

Personhood is in the piece even when the vocabulary is diplomatic. The Taliban's record on women, on dissent, on the right to appear in public as a full legal being, is why the word vile is not a flourish. Engagement does not wash that record. It admits that the people living under it cannot be reached only by a press release from a capital that no longer has an embassy. Mining and trade will happen with or without a Western blessing; the only question is whether democracies keep a pair of eyes and a phone number in the country, or outsource both to Moscow, Beijing, Delhi, Ankara, and Abu Dhabi. Five years is long enough to call the experiment. Hardliners who do not need your investment will not become kinder because you withheld it. Read the original as statecraft, not as a conversion narrative. The magazine is not asking you to like the men in Kabul. It is asking you to stop confusing a snub with a strategy, and to remember that recognition is a tool, not a hug.

Read the leader. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: isolation that changes nothing is not purity. It is a vacant chair.

articles.title: America Inc has a tight grip on allied governments
articles.summary: 从 Palantir 到洛克希德，美国公司卡住了盟国政府：想少依赖，换起来却极贵。
articles.briefing:
From Palantir to Lockheed, American firms take only a small share of allied government spending and remain extraordinarily hard to replace. That is the Economist's business-page paradox, and it is more interesting than a rant about empire. The money is not the whole grip. The grip is criticality. Once a ministry's intelligence stack, or a military's aircraft, or a border agency's database is built around a particular American vendor, switching is not a procurement preference. It is a years-long risk to readiness: training, spare parts, classified interfaces, the unglamorous lock-in that never appears in a speech about sovereignty. Allies say they want less dependence. They also want the systems that work this year. Those two wants do not sit on the same purchase order. A small invoice can still be the one you cannot tear up.

Donald Trump uses firms as statecraft. That is not a new American habit — arms exports have always been diplomacy by other means — but the present mood is closer to gunboat capitalism than to the older language of an open commercial order. A company can be a favour, a threat, a channel, a punishment. Allies who dislike the politics still need the product. The product, in the cases that matter, is not a commodity. There is no equivalent shelf of Palantir-like software or Lockheed-like platforms that a mid-sized democracy can adopt on a Tuesday without losing a capability it has already promised its own public. The small share of the budget is the camouflage. A line item can look modest and still be the hinge on which a state's capacity turns. That is a tighter grip than a large, replaceable contract.

The essay's discipline, which this briefing will copy, is not to invent revenue numbers. The argument does not need a fake billion. It needs the structure: concentrated capability, high switching costs, a White House willing to treat private firms as instruments, and a set of allies who talk diversification while signing the next contract. Europe's talk of strategic autonomy, and everyone else's talk of "de-risking," meets the same wall. You can want a second supplier. You cannot will one into existence at the same level of integration, on the same timetable as a crisis. Meanwhile the political price of the first supplier rises. Dependence that was once described as alliance is starting to feel like exposure. That feeling is the business story, and it is the political one.

This issue's theme is proof and personhood; the business rhyme is sovereignty. A government that cannot see, fly, or file without a firm headquartered in another capital is a government whose personhood as a state is leased. That does not make Palantir or Lockheed villains in a comic. It makes the bargain visible. The tech is critical, which is why the switching cost is not a consultant's slide but a fear of going dark. Trump's willingness to treat the firms as instruments raises the political rent on a dependence that already existed. Allies can want a second stack. They cannot pretend the first one is optional while the planes still need parts and the database still needs the vendor who built it. Read the original for the cases and the tone. The Economist is not writing a manifesto against American technology. It is describing a market that has become a political fact, and a politics that has become a market — gunboat capitalism with invoices.

Read the piece. This briefing is here so the grip is already in the room: a small share of spending, a large share of the things a state cannot do without.

articles.title: Vesuvius Revisited
articles.summary: 公元 79 年是三场灾难，不是一张明信片；基恩用 DNA 和人工智能重访维苏威底下的人。
articles.briefing:
Sam Kean's National Geographic feature asks you to stop treating AD 79 as a single postcard of a city under ash. Vesuvius produced three disasters that day, or rather three different deaths from one mountain. Pompeii was buried in lapilli, a rain of volcanic stone about ten feet deep, a death by burial and heat and falling sky. Herculaneum was hit by pyroclastic currents, a ground-hugging storm of gas and rock that stacked some sixty feet of material and carbonized papyrus scrolls instead of simply burning them to nothing. Oplontis took both: a villa landscape and, in a storeroom, dozens of skeletons. The usual tourist sentence — Pompeii, ash, plaster casts — is not false. It is a third of the event, and the least interesting third if you care about what can still be read out of the dead. Kean's revisit is a reminder that one eruption can file people in three different archives.

New tools have turned the sites into laboratories of personhood. Artificial intelligence and DNA do not resurrect anyone. They do something almost as uncanny: they sort the anonymous. Skeletons in the Oplontis storeroom can be read for class and gender, which is a polite way of saying that a heap of bones was a set of lives with different access to food, labour, and the chance to run. A Pompeii latrine becomes a genomic study of diet and health, which is a polite way of saying that excrement is an archive. The Herculaneum scrolls, carbonized and long unreadable, are being virtually unwrapped: layers inferred, letters recovered, a library that fire preserved by destroying it as an object. Paolo Verzone's photographs keep the science from floating free of the rooms. You are still looking at a storeroom, a latrine, a charred roll.

The scientific temptation is to make 79 a demo reel. Kean's better instinct, if you follow the structure, is to keep the three sites distinct so that method has something to bite. A pyroclastic current and a lapilli fall are not the same taphonomy. They hide and reveal different things. DNA that speaks to sex and status in a storeroom is not the same as a scroll that may yet yield a sentence of philosophy. Both are ways of refusing the mountain the last word. The dead were not a genre. They were people who ate, owned or served in a villa, used a latrine, kept books. Recovering that is not sentiment. It is the opposite of the plaster-cast aesthetic, which turns a body into a shape for a postcard.

This issue keeps asking who is recorded as human. Vesuvius recorded everyone and no one: a perfect catastrophe, a terrible archive. The new work is a second recording. It says: this skeleton was not a type; this diet was not "the ancients"; this scroll was a text someone meant to read again. AI here is a tool for unwrapping and sorting, not a personality. DNA is a tool for giving a storeroom back its class structure and its sexes. Together they make Oplontis more than a villa with extra bones, Pompeii more than a latrine joke, Herculaneum more than a carbonized rumour of a library. Read Kean for the three disasters and for the labs. The original has the space to keep the sites from collapsing into one word, and Verzone's photographs keep the rooms from becoming a methods section. This briefing is the map. The mountain did not write a single story. We are only now learning how to read the three.

Read the National Geographic piece. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room.

articles.title: Physicists find major clue to matter’s biggest mystery
articles.summary: 物质为何压过反物质：STAR 把重子数追到 Y 形胶子结，而不是三个价夸克那么简单。
articles.briefing:
Why is there something rather than a neat cancellation? In the early universe, matter and antimatter should have destroyed each other into light. A residue of matter remained, and we are that residue's later gossip. Scientific American reports a clue from STAR, a detector at Brookhaven's Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider — a machine that was shut down earlier in 2026, which gives the result the mood of a last letter. The clue is not a new philosophy of Being. It is a claim about how baryon number, the accounting rule that says protons and neutrons are "matter" in the everyday sense, might actually be carried. Not only by three valence quarks, the textbook picture on a coffee mug, but by a Y-shaped junction of gluons, the particles that hold quarks together. Zhangbu Xu, Rongrong Ma, and Dmitri Kharzeev are among the names on the work. The paper is in Science. A major clue, in this register, is a better picture of the bookkeeping, not a hymn.

The experimental cunning is almost more interesting than the metaphysics. STAR collided nuclei of ruthenium and of zirconium: the same mass number, different charge. That pairing is a way of separating the transport of electric charge from the transport of baryon number. If the two moved differently, you have a handle on whether "being a baryon" is just a quark-counting exercise or something lodged in the glue. A Y-shaped gluon junction is a strange object to ask a general reader to love. Love it anyway, at least as an idea. It says that the extra-ness of matter — the thing that gets conserved when particles rearrange — may live in a topology of force rather than in three little balls. The universe's leftover stuff would then be leftover structure.

This does not answer Heidegger. The magazine's headline will tempt a certain kind of reader to think that physics has now explained why there is a world. It has not. It has traced, more carefully, how a conservation law might be implemented in the debris of a collider that no longer runs. That is a major clue to matter's biggest mystery only if you keep the mystery in its scientific size: the asymmetry, the accounting, the junction. The human-sized mystery — why this, why us, why a week of magazines — remains untouched, which is a relief. A result can be important without being a worldview. STAR's last useful gift may be exactly that: a narrower, better question about glue, asked before the collider went quiet.

Personhood is a long way from a gluon. The rhyme, if you want one for this issue, is modest. We are here because the cancellation was imperfect. The experiment tries to say where the imperfection hides in the bookkeeping. Ruthenium versus zirconium is a clean trick: hold mass still, vary charge, watch what travels. If baryon number rides a Y of glue, the leftover world is leftover architecture. Xu, Ma, and Kharzeev are doing collider physics, not metaphysics, and the shutdown of RHIC earlier this year makes the Science paper feel like a result that has to stand without a sequel on the same machine. Read the original for the detector, the isotopes, and the caution that a clue is not a closing argument. This briefing is here so you do not walk in expecting a solution to existence. You are walking in on a paper about how baryon number is conserved, written as the machine that tested it goes dark.

Read Scientific American. The argument is already in the room: matter's surplus may be a shape in the glue.

articles.title: Sasquatch science
articles.summary: 大脚怪爱好者其实很empiricist：他们在科学制度外头工作，一旦成功就会被科学吞进去。
articles.briefing:
Jamie Lewis and Andrew Bartlett did not go into the woods to believe. They went, for Bigfooters and Scientific Inquiry (2026), to watch a scene that institutional science prefers to treat as a joke. More than a hundred and sixty interviews later, the joke is less useful than the sociology. Bigfooters are often empiricists. They use environmental DNA. They put hair under microscopes. They argue about contamination, chain of custody, and what would count as a type specimen. They are not, as a class, enemies of method. They are outside the institutions that get to say which objects are worth a method. George Eberhart's advice, which the essay takes seriously, is to apply a scientific or a journalistic procedure and see what survives. The subject is not a ghost and not a UFO. A great ape in the temperate forest would not rewrite physics. It would rewrite a range map.

That last point is the intellectual hygiene of the piece. If your anomaly requires the violation of conservation laws, you are in a different business. If your anomaly is a large primate that official biology has not admitted, you are making a claim that could, in principle, be absorbed. The irony, which Lewis and Bartlett do not waste, is that success would abolish the subculture. A verified Sasquatch becomes a mammal. Journals would take it. Museums would skin it. The people who spent weekends in the rain would be remembered as amateurs who happened to be right, or they would be forgotten, which is how science treats its borderlands once the border moves. Failure, meanwhile, is not a single event. It is a lifetime of prints, films, and hairs that never quite close the case. The methods can be scientific while the community remains a community of the unincluded.

The essay is therefore not a brief for Bigfoot. It is a study of what inquiry looks like when it cannot get a grant, a referee, or a polite hearing. That should interest anyone who cares about how knowledge is policed. Institutions are right to be expensive with their attention. They are also capable of confusing prestige with warrant. Bigfooters can be credulous, territorial, and wrong in the ordinary human ways. They can also be more careful with a sample than a television documentary will ever show. The interesting object is the border: a place where people use the tools of science without the permission structure of science. Call it the sociology of the almost-discipline.

This week's theme is proof. Few subjects are more purely about proof than a creature that may not exist. What would count. Who is allowed to bring the evidence. Why a hair is never enough. The contrast with STAR's gluon junction is almost comic and still exact. One community has a collider and a journal. The other has a creek and a mailing list. Both are trying to bind a claim to a method. eDNA and microscopy are not spells; they are the same family of tools a wildlife biologist would use for a less embarrassing animal. Eberhart's fork — scientific or journalistic method — is a way of staying honest when the academy will not host you. Read Lewis and Bartlett for the hundred-plus interviews, not for a monster. The original will not make you a believer. It may make you slower to use "unscientific" as a social insult rather than a description of a procedure. If they ever succeeded, the irony would complete itself: science would absorb the ape and forget the scene that found it.

Read the Aeon essay. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: the borderlands of science are still using science. That is what makes them awkward.

articles.title: An AI for Africa would be built on Hunhu/Ubuntu ethics
articles.summary: 为非洲做的人工智能应从乌班图出发：人因他人而为人，而不是把用户当成主权个体。
articles.briefing:
Western AI, in the story this Aeon essay tells, treats the user as a sovereign individual. The community appears later, if it appears, as an aggregate of data points: users, engagement, a market. Hunhu, in Shona, and Ubuntu, in the Nguni languages, start somewhere else. A person is a person through other people — umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu. John Mbiti's compression is the one that travels: "I am because we are." John Pobee's Latin joke, Cognatus ergo sum, makes the same claim against the ghost of Descartes. You do not begin as a thinking atom and then join a group. You begin already related. An AI built as if that were true would not be a reskin of a Californian product with a proverb in the splash screen. It would change what the system is for: whose problem it is allowed to notice, and whom it must answer when it fails.

The inversion is practical. Start from community need rather than from a user who must be retained. Prioritise collective agency: what a village, a clinic network, a language group can do together that no single account-holder can do. Aim at a common good that can be argued about in public, not at a personalised feed that cannot. Build accountability to the communities the system affects, including the ones that will never be "customers." Take on environmental and intergenerational duty, because a model that burns power and harvests data is already a decision about the unborn and about land. None of this is a guarantee of virtue. Collectives can be cruel. Elders can be wrong. The point is the unit of moral concern. If the unit is the sovereign user, the harms that count are harms to that user. If the unit is the we, a different ledger opens, and design has to follow the ledger or the ethics is only branding.

Data colonialism is the warning that keeps the essay from becoming a greeting card. African lives, voices, and images are already training other people's systems, often without a political relationship that looks like consent. A Ubuntu vocabulary can be stolen as easily as a dataset. The test is not whether a firm can quote Mbiti. The test is whether design, ownership, and recourse begin from the community that will live with the outputs. Otherwise "AI for Africa" is an export market with better morals in the keynote. The essay's wager is that the philosophical resources are already local — Hunhu, Ubuntu, a long argument about what a person is — and that importing only the individualist user-model is itself a political choice, not a technical necessity.

This issue's keystone, later, is a machine that wants to prove you are a human individual. Ubuntu is the useful friction. Proof of humanity, in that other story, is a scan, a unique ID, a person separated from the crowd. Proof of humanity here is relational: you are someone because you are among others, answerable to them, unfinished without them. Mbiti and Pobee are not decoration for a keynote. They are a different starting axiom from the sovereign user. Hunhu and Ubuntu name that axiom in languages that had it before the platform did. Read the original for the ethics as a design brief, not as a slogan. This briefing is the inversion. The essay is where it has to survive contact with servers, contracts, and the old extractive habit of taking African data to train someone else's I.

Read Aeon. The argument is already in the room: an African AI that begins from I think, therefore I am, has already chosen its continent.

articles.title: Scientists are using AI to design new viruses. Should they be?
articles.summary: 斯坦福用人工智能设计出能杀死耐药大肠杆菌的噬菌体：有用，也已经跑在监管前面。
articles.briefing:
The question in Scientific American's headline is not rhetorical decoration. Researchers at Stanford and the Arc Institute trained Evo 1 and Evo 2 on millions of bacteriophage genomes — viruses that infect bacteria, not people — and then asked the models to design new ones, using the tiny phage ΦX174 as a template. Thousands of designs came out. About 302 were synthesised. Sixteen proved viable. Some of those can kill strains of E. coli that shrug off antibiotics. The models were not trained on human-infecting viruses, a boundary the paper can state and a successor project can erase. The work appeared in Science, after a 2025 preprint, which is another way of saying that the research has been in the open long enough for the commentary to catch up and not long enough for the law to. Tom Inglesby and a colleague, Hanke, write on the biosecurity problem. The useful therapy and the misuse risk arrive in the same paragraph, which is how a capability looks before a rulebook exists.

Phage therapy is the hopeful reading, and it is not a fantasy. Antibiotic resistance is a present killer. A virus that eats a bacterium is an old idea with a new design tool. If a model can propose genomes that wet labs can then test, the search space gets larger than a graduate student's intuition. The sixteen viable phages are a proof of generation, not a pharmacy. They are also a proof that "design" is no longer only a human with a pipette imagining a tweak. The machine proposes; the bench still has to build and see what lives. That division of labour will not stay polite. It will get faster.

The darker reading does not require a screenwriter. If someone fine-tunes similar models on pathogens that infect humans, the same pipeline — propose, synthesise, test — becomes a problem that existing regulation was not written to see. Inglesby and Hanke's commentary is the adult voice in the room: capability is outrunning the rules that assume a slower, more human-scale biology. This briefing will not rehearse a method. The magazine's job is the policy tension. Research that is openly useful for drug-resistant infections is also a demonstration that genomic models can invent viable viruses. The demonstration cannot be unpublished. It can be governed, or it can be left to the ethics of whoever has a synthesis budget and a reason. That is the "should they" in the title, and it will not get quieter.

Should they be doing this? The piece will not give you a chant. It will give you a field that has already moved. A digest for a university reader should keep both goods in view: a possible tool against resistant bacteria, and a reminder that "not trained on human viruses" is a choice, not a law of nature. ΦX174 is a small, well-known template; the jump from a famous tiny phage to sixteen living designs is the part that makes the headline true. Thousands generated, a few hundred built, a handful alive: that funnel is now a fact, and regulation is still catching the preprint from 2025. Personhood returns as vulnerability. We are bodies that can be infected, and we are also the species that now writes infection as a prompt. Read the original for the Science paper, the Inglesby and Hanke commentary, and the timeline. This briefing is here so the question is already in the room, which is the only honest place to leave it.

Read Scientific American. The research is ahead of the rulebook. The essay is where that fact has to be faced.

articles.title: Are You a Human?
articles.summary: 利波尔写证明你是人的历史：从 CAPTCHA 到奥布，问题已变成好机器人与坏机器人。
articles.briefing:
Jill Lepore's New Yorker essay is this issue's keystone, and it should be read as history rather than as a gadget review. Sam Altman posted a video on X: people queue in a city that looks like Nagoya to stare into the Orb, a device from Tools for Humanity, the company he shares with Alex Blania. The product is Proof of Humanity. You give the machine your iris, or your face, or whatever the orb has decided counts, and you receive a token that says you are not a bot. The scene is already a parable. A line of bodies, a spherical judge, a Silicon Valley firm in the business of certifying the species. Lepore's gift is to refuse the parable's newness. We have been proving we are human for a long time. The props change. The anxiety does not.

CAPTCHA is the ancestor most readers have already failed at a traffic light. Moni Naor floated the idea in 1996. Luis von Ahn, at Carnegie Mellon, named it and made it a puzzle. reCAPTCHA arrived with a slogan that now reads like an epitaph for a certain internet: "STOP SPAM. READ BOOKS." Google bought the company in 2009 and used the leftover human labour to digitise books, which is a joke so exact it feels invented and is not. You proved you were a person by typing a word a scanner could not read. The books got a free workforce. Invisible reCAPTCHA later stopped asking so many questions and started watching behaviour: how you move the mouse, how you time a click, the mess that a body makes and a script does not. Humans are messy. Bots are tidy. The tests got better at finding tidiness, and the bots got better at faking mess.

Now there are more bots than people online, and the interesting problem is no longer human versus machine. It is good bots versus bad bots, and humans caught in the sorting. A proof-of-humanity orb is a late answer to an old administrative hunger: brands on skin, papers at a border, an iris at a gate. Lepore walks that history without needing to invent a single extra station. Identity, once a matter of being known in a place, became a matter of being scannable by a system that does not know you. The Orb is only the latest instrument that wants a unique body to underwrite a unique account. Whether you find that liberating — a defence against spam, deepfakes, a web of clones — or find it a new enclosure of the eye, the essay will not let you treat it as a product launch.

The week's other pieces keep colliding with this one. Beckett hid a person in a notebook because a state was redefining who counted. Arendt arrived without a state and spent a life on what that does to judgment. Ubuntu says a person is a person through other people, which is almost the opposite of an iris that isolates you as a successful scan. Roberts's Court is being asked who is a citizen at birth. Lepore is asking who is a human on a network. The questions are not the same. They share a nervous system. Proof is never only technical. It is a decision about which kind of evidence a world will accept, and who is locked out when the evidence changes.

Read the original when you have a long sitting. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room. The magazine's job is the full walk, from Naor to the Orb, including the parts a digest would only flatten.

articles.title: The Doulas Who Help Us Die
articles.summary: 临终导乐做的不是医疗，是在场：张、肖克和阿克陪伴人把最后一段走完。
articles.briefing:
Virginia Chang works in New York as an end-of-life doula, which is a job title that still sounds like a category error to people who think doulas belong only to birth. The New Yorker's feature stays with her long enough for the error to fade. She does a street ritual she describes as becoming an empty vessel. There is a Sanskrit mantra. There are red clogs. She entered the work after losing people she loved, which is the least surprising origin story in the profession and still the one that has to be told, because presence of this kind is not a career one picks from a brochure. Jill Schock, in Los Angeles, came from chaplaincy. Emma Acker is in the piece as a reminder that some clients cannot afford fees. The work is not medicine. It is a profession of presence: sitting, arranging, witnessing, keeping a death from being only a set of clinical events in a room that is trying to stay on schedule.

Photographs by Lauren Lancaster and Stella Kalinina do part of the reporting. A doula's labour is hard to quote. It is posture, time, the refusal to flee the ordinary ugliness of a body shutting down. Magazines like a mystic. The better version of this story is plainer. Hospitals are built to treat. Families are often untrained for the last week. A doula is someone who will still be there when the treatment conversation is over and the person is not. Chang's ritual language — vessel, mantra, the clogs as a kind of uniform — will strike some readers as theatre. It may also be how a worker protects a psyche that has to enter other people's endings for a living. Schock's chaplain past makes the continuity obvious. Sacred attention migrated out of the hospital's official chapel and into a freelance practice with an invoice.

Money is the unspiritual fact the piece is right to include. If presence is a profession, it has a price, and the price will sort the dying. Acker’s clients who cannot pay are not a subplot. They are the proof that a humane death, in a market society, becomes another service. That does not make the doulas hypocrites. It makes the work visible as labour. Birth doulas already taught this lesson: intimacy can be skilled, skilled work can be charged, and the people who most need the skill are often the ones who cannot buy it. Death is not more equal. It is only more final.

Personhood at the end of life is this issue's last, quiet version of the theme. A dying person can stop being treated as a speaker and become a problem of management: pain, paperwork, the family's logistics. A doula's claim is that the speaker is still there, or that the body still deserves an audience. You do not have to want a Sanskrit mantra, or to like red clogs, to want that. Chang's empty-vessel ritual and Schock's former chapel are two dialects of the same job: stay. Lancaster and Kalinina's photographs will do what prose should not — show the rooms without turning them into a lesson. Read the original for those rooms. This briefing will not restage a death. It will say what kind of article you are opening: a study of people who stay, in a culture that is better at machines for proving we are human than at sitting with the moment when the proof stops mattering.

Read the New Yorker when you have a long sitting. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room. Presence is the product. Medicine is someone else's job.

articles.title: Signal then storm
articles.summary: 巴斯鲍姆找了五十年慢性痛的源头：痛是主观的，他仍赌外周驱动，而不是先改大脑。
articles.briefing:
Stephani Sutherland's Aeon essay is a fifty-year hunt with a living hunter. Allan Basbaum is seventy-eight, at UCSF, and he has spent his career on the circuits of pain. The title's weather is his sequence: a signal, then a storm. Something happens at the edge of the body. The central nervous system can amplify it, rewrite it, make it permanent. The clinical culture he is arguing with often starts in the brain, or in the mind, because pain is subjective and subjectivity looks like a psychological fact. Basbaum does not deny the subjectivity. He denies the leap. Pain is molecular as well as felt. He wants to interrupt peripheral drivers before the brain has made a career of them. Treatment that begins in the brain, on his wager, is often treatment that has arrived after the plot has thickened — useful, sometimes, and late if the first fire is still burning in the tissue.

His line, which the essay is right to keep, is not a slogan for patients to shout at doctors. "Just because you don't know where [the peripheral injury] is, doesn't mean it doesn't exist." Chronic pain is full of cases in which imaging is clean and the person is not. The clean image becomes a social verdict: if we cannot see it, perhaps it is not the body. Basbaum's bet is the opposite of a dismissal. The injury, the nociceptor, the quiet damage, may be real and still unnamed. The brain can worsen pain and can improve it; he does not pretend the centre is a passenger. He still puts his money on a peripheral driver, because that is where a cause might be cut before the storm learns to generate its own weather.

Fifty years is long enough for a field to change religions more than once. Pain has been a stimulus, a gate, a neuromatrix, a biopsychosocial bundle, an opioid market, a crisis. Basbaum's stubbornness is a research programme, not a mood. Map the circuit. Find the molecules. Ask whether the periphery is still talking. A university reader who has been trained to hear "subjective" as "less real" needs this essay as a correction. Subjective is how pain is known. It is not a proof that the known thing is imaginary. The correction matters outside the clinic. A person in pain is one of the hardest cases of proof: they have a report, and the world wants a picture. When the picture fails, the person is downgraded. His sentence about the unseen injury is a refusal of that downgrade.

Sutherland writes a scientist, not a saint. The piece will have the labs, the decades, the arguments with colleagues who prefer a central story. Basbaum at seventy-eight is not a mascot for stoicism; he is a man who still thinks the interesting cut is at the periphery, where a molecular event can be interrupted before the cord and the cortex have learned the plot. Pain remains subjective — only the person has the storm — and still, on his account, molecular. This briefing keeps the hinge. Signal, then storm. Look for the signal. Do not let the storm's complexity become an excuse to stop looking, and do not let a blank scan become a moral judgment on the reporter. Read the original when you have a sitting. Aeon will give you the career. The argument is already in the room: the brain is powerful, and the edge of the body is still where he would like to stop the story from starting.

Read the essay. This briefing is the wager. The fifty years are in the piece.

articles.title: Why loneliness and not social isolation may be making you sick
articles.summary: 让人生病的更可能是孤独感，而不是社交隔离：这项三角研究不支持心脏病头条。
articles.briefing:
The World Health Organisation's figure is the one that will travel: about one in six people are lonely. Scientific American's piece is more useful than the figure, because it refuses to treat loneliness and social isolation as the same illness. Loneliness is distress: the gap between the relationships you have and the connection you wanted. Isolation is a count — how many contacts, how often. The two can diverge. You can be busy with people and lonely. You can live thinly and not mind. A public-health conversation that collapses them will prescribe the wrong thing: more events for people whose problem is not a calendar, or a pep talk about "reaching out" for people whose problem is an empty week. The title's "may" is doing honest work. This is not a licence to diagnose a planet from one study.

A new triangulation study — observational data, sibling controls, Mendelian randomisation; UK Biobank plus GWAS — tries to pull the strands apart. Loneliness, in this work, is linked to depression, to the risk of self-harm and suicide attempt, to lower life satisfaction, and to multimorbidity, the pile-up of conditions that makes a life medical. Isolation's clearest effect is poorer wellbeing. What the study does not give you, and what a certain kind of headline will try to steal anyway, is a consistent effect on coronary artery disease, heart failure, stroke, systolic blood pressure, or type 2 diabetes. This briefing will not invent a heart-attack lead. The heart is not the story the data will securely tell. The mind, the mood, the stacked diagnoses, the wish to be done with living: those are the associations that hold still long enough to report. That list is already grave enough without a fake infarct.

Mendelian randomisation and sibling controls are the authors' attempt to be less fooled by confounders. People who are lonely may also be poor, unwell, or already depressed in ways that confuse a simple correlation. The methods are not magic. They are a way of saying: we tried to ask whether the loneliness is doing work, or only travelling with the work. A reader does not need to pretend to have parsed every instrument variable. A reader does need to keep the conclusion in its size. Loneliness looks like a mental-health and multimorbidity problem more than like a straightforward vascular one, at least here. Isolation looks like a wellbeing problem. Policy that buys blood-pressure cuffs for the lonely and ignores the distress is reading last decade's op-ed.

Personhood, again, is the felt fact. Isolation counts your contacts as if a person were a node. Loneliness asks whether the node is a life. The WHO number is a crowd: one in six, a size that makes ministers hold summits. The study is a distinction, and the distinction is the only reason to read past the summit. Sibling controls and Mendelian randomisation will not make the result eternal; they make it harder to wave away as "lonely people were already sick." They also do not license a story about hearts and strokes that the associations will not carry. Read the original for the design and the caution. This briefing is here so you do not walk out with a fake cardiology lesson. The sickness, if the paper is right, is more about how badly the wanted world mismatches the actual one — depression, self-harm, the stacked diagnoses, the drop in satisfaction — than about a heart that failed because nobody called.

Read Scientific American. The argument is already in the room: count the contacts if you want; measure the distress if you want to know why people are unwell.
